title: Signed Language Awareness (ASL in a Canadian Context)
summary: By the end, learners can name the signed languages recognized in federal accessibility law, explain that ASL and LSQ are real languages, describe why a qualified interpreter is different from a friend who “knows some signs,” outline what Canada’s Video Relay Service is for, and find official places to learn more — without treating this course as interpreter training.
goals: By the end, learners can name the signed languages recognized in federal accessibility law, explain that ASL and LSQ are real languages, describe why a qualified interpreter is different from a friend who “knows some signs,” outline what Canada’s Video Relay Service is for, and find official places to learn more — without treating this course as interpreter training.
certificateNote: It is not a college diploma, degree, trade ticket, professional licence, or sign-language interpreter certification.

lessons.title: What this course is, and which languages the law names
lessons.html:
Signed languages are languages. People use their hands, face, and body to share meaning. This course explains that idea in a Canadian context. It does not teach you enough ASL to interpret a meeting, a medical appointment, or a legal matter.

The Accessible Canada Act is a federal law. The Department of Justice text of section 5.1 says American Sign Language, Quebec Sign Language, and Indigenous sign languages are recognized as the primary languages for communication by deaf persons in Canada. A Government of Canada summary of the Act uses the French name Langue des signes québécoise (LSQ) for Quebec Sign Language. That summary also says the purpose of the Act is to make Canada barrier-free by January 1, 2040, in areas that include communication.

“Primary language” here means these signed languages are recognized in that law as the main languages Deaf people use to communicate in Canada. It does not mean every Deaf person uses the same language, and it does not make you an interpreter.

The same Government of Canada summary notes that Canada already has a human-rights framework that includes the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the Canadian Human Rights Act, and Canada’s commitments under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. This course does not interpret those laws for your situation.

If you want to learn to sign, look for classes taught by qualified Deaf teachers after you finish these awareness lessons.

lessons.title: ASL and LSQ are real languages
lessons.html:
The Canadian Association of the Deaf – Association des Sourds du Canada (CAD-ASC) is a national Deaf organization. On its language position page it says the natural language of Deaf people is Sign language, and that in Canada there are two legitimate Sign languages: American Sign Language (ASL) and la Langue des Signes Quebecoise (LSQ). It also notes a regional dialect called Maritimes Sign Language (MSL).

CAD-ASC describes these Sign languages as real languages with their own grammar, syntax, and vocabulary. They are not “English on the hands” or “French on the hands.” A word-for-word signed copy of an English sentence is not the same thing as ASL.

On its official-languages page, CAD-ASC says it uses ASL and LSQ as its two official languages, with English and French as secondary languages. It also says captioning, lip-reading, assistive devices, and oral interpretation are other ways some people access language, but those modes are not the same as ASL or LSQ.

You cannot assume every Deaf person lip-reads, speaks, or uses the same signed language. A person in much of English-speaking Canada may use ASL. A person in Quebec may use LSQ. Some people use more than one language. Some people are Deafblind and may use other tactile or visual ways to communicate.

This lesson is awareness, not a grammar class. Do not invent signs from English word order and call it ASL.

lessons.title: Qualified interpreters are not “a friend who knows some signs”
lessons.html:
A professional interpreter’s job is to relay communication between people who do not share a language. Finishing this course does not give you that skill.

CAD-ASC’s interpreting page says qualified professional interpreting helps non-Deaf people communicate with Deaf people. It supports using qualified professional interpreters who belong to the interpreter associations named on that page. It does not consider family, friends, acquaintances, social workers, teachers, educational assistants, ministers, or others to be qualified professional interpreters.

CAD-ASC also says interpreters (except Deaf interpreters and Deaf intervenors) are not experts or consultants on Deaf issues. They facilitate communication. Expertise on Deaf issues and Deaf culture comes from Deaf people themselves.

If your workplace, clinic, or council meeting needs signed-language access, arrange a qualified interpreter. Do not ask a co-worker’s child, a neighbour, or “someone who took a short course” to interpret an important conversation. That can leave out information and put private details in the wrong hands.

Skills for Success collaboration includes valuing diversity and working respectfully with people who have different abilities and ways of communicating. Government of Canada accessibility guidance also says organizations should consider offering materials in ASL, LSQ, or Indigenous sign languages, and should plan time for interpreter requests.

If you are speaking with a Deaf person through an interpreter, talk with the person, not about them as if they were not there. Wait for the interpreter to finish. This course still does not make you that interpreter.

lessons.title: Canada’s Video Relay Service
lessons.html:
Canada has a national Video Relay Service, often called Canada VRS. It is administered by the Canadian Administrator of Video Relay Service (CAV), a not-for-profit organization mandated by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC).

Canada VRS’s own pages say the service lets Deaf, DeafBlind, hard-of-hearing, and other Canadians who use ASL or LSQ as their primary language communicate with voice telephone users through internet video. A sign-language interpreter relays the conversation in real time between signed language and spoken language.

The service is free to use. To register, you must be a primary sign language user. After you register, you receive a personal VRS number so you can make and receive calls. CAV says Canada VRS launched on September 28, 2016, and is available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. Apps are described for iOS, Android, Windows, and Mac computers.

Government of Canada accessibility guidance describes VRS in similar terms: a person using sign language can make telephone and videoconference calls through an operator who interprets their signing verbally, and the other way around.

VRS is a telephone-access tool. It is not the same as booking an in-person interpreter for a long meeting, and this course does not register you for the service. Hearing colleagues who are not primary sign language users should not treat the VRS app as their own interpreter training.

For help, Canada VRS lists support@srvcanadavrs.ca and 1-800-958-5856 (English and French). Always check the live page, because contact details can change.

lessons.title: Where to learn more, and what this course is not
lessons.html:
If signed languages matter in your work or community, keep learning from official and Deaf-led sources.

Useful starting points:

  • The Accessible Canada Act text and the Government of Canada summary, for the legal recognition of ASL, LSQ, and Indigenous sign languages
  • CAD-ASC (cad-asc.ca), for national Deaf-community positions on language and interpreting
  • Canada VRS (srvcanadavrs.ca), if you or someone you support is a primary ASL or LSQ user who needs to make a voice telephone call
  • Local Deaf organizations and classes taught by qualified Deaf teachers. CAD-ASC says qualified Deaf teachers should teach Sign language

Government of Canada guidance on consulting persons with disabilities uses the principle “Nothing without us.” That means Deaf people should be involved when programs and services are designed, not only talked about after decisions are made.

Do not:

  • Pretend this five-lesson awareness course is interpreter training
  • Use a family member as a professional interpreter for important or private conversations
  • Invent signs and call them ASL or LSQ
  • Assume one signed language works for every Deaf person in Canada

A respectful next step is simple: learn whose language is being used, arrange proper access when it is needed, and keep studying with people who are qualified to teach.

keptBack.sourceDisclaimer: This course is general awareness about signed languages in Canada. It is not American Sign Language (ASL) fluency training, not an interpreter certificate, and not a substitute for learning from qualified Deaf teachers or professional interpreters. It is not legal, medical, or human-rights advice about a person’s case. Do not treat a few facts from this course as enough skill to interpret for someone.
